extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially fantasy authors) designing magic systems
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for authors on designing consistent, interesting magic systems for fiction, focusing on how limitations, weaknesses, and costs produce better story conflict, character development, and worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations > Powers (Sanderson's Second Law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations are more important than the powers themselves; design magic by emphasizing what it can't or won't do rather than only what it can do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated succinctly as 'Limitations > Powers.' Use examples (Superman: powers vs. kryptonite and code of ethics) to show that weaknesses/limits define interest. The law is a writing principle: originality often lies in limitations rather than the power concept. Applied broadly to characters, worldbuilding, and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: A good limitation forces characters to work for their goals, making scenes more interesting and characters more sympathetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design limitations that require characters to be clever and active (example: Mistborn's metal-only telekinesis with push/pull rules and weight consequences). This encourages tighter scenes and forces the writer to craft more inventive solutions rather than hand-waving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations increase narrative tension by introducing stakes and vulnerability where raw power would remove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limitations/weaknesses to create risk in confrontations (Superman vs. kryptonite; Batman's psychological vulnerabilities). Avoid making conflicts trivial by giving characters guaranteed power without trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-designed limitations add depth by tying abilities to character psychology, plot, and world—making powers meaningful beyond utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a character who can fly only when happy ties an ability to mood and therefore to character development and plot. Limitations should encourage authors to expand world detail and character backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations (definition & design guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations are things the magic simply cannot do; they define scope and should be consistent and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond simple numeric bounds to craft limitations that evoke the nature of the magic (example: Will and the Word cannot 'unmake' things). Consistency is crucial; rationality is desirable but consistency matters most. Tie limitations to the world's cosmology and use them to force creative problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaknesses (definition & cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weaknesses are vulnerabilities opponents can exploit—distinct from neutral limitations—and should be used carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic or clichéd weaknesses (e.g., 'lose powers in sunlight' as lazy fix). Make weaknesses subtle and story-relevant—ways magic makes users vulnerable rather than obvious, mechanical handicaps. Treat weaknesses as bridges between limitations and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs (definition & balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs are consequences for using or associating with magic; they can be abstract (insanity) or concrete (consumable resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs are expected by readers and create real trade-offs (Wheel of Time: men go insane; Dune: spice as fuel). Balance costs so they are meaningful but not so severe they prevent use (avoid crippling costs like 'using a spell kills a grandparent' unless you accept narrative limits). Distinguish whether the cost is author-locked (concrete) or flexible/interpretive (abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: How magic is accessed (innate vs. learned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether magic is innate, learned, or a hybrid—this choice shapes character arcs and world dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varying access methods can make a system stand out; innate systems imply different social/political implications than learned systems. Use access mechanics to generate conflict, social structure, or plot hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power source and conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define what powers the magic and how it interacts with physics (energy source, where matter/energy goes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider conservation of energy/thermodynamics analogies to avoid implausible 'infinite creation.' Typical sources include willpower or an external universal force. Explicitly stating power sources can tie magic to cosmology and create interesting limits or costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage frequency, implements, and special states
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify how often magic can be used and whether it requires implements, special mental states, or ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If requirements are cosmetic (implements that never affect plot), they weaken the system. Make usage constraints meaningful to plot, economics, or character behavior (e.g., rare components, limited daily uses, ritual states). Avoid trivial 'rules' that exist only as hand-waving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency over rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: The magic system must be consistent; it need not be fully 'rational' so long as its rules hold within the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency allows foil for problem-solving and foreshadowing. Even if internal logic is fantastic, maintain rules so limitations and costs are believable and usable for plot development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid solving plot problems by changing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not add new powers or remove limitations solely to get characters out of narrative difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist deus ex machina: keep to rules to encourage inventive solutions. If rules change, make it a plot point that is properly foreshadowed or earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make limitations have narrative consequences (no cosmetic limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations should affect characters and plot in tangible, meaningful ways rather than being superficial constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design limits that produce ethical dilemmas, economic effects, or character development; avoid limits that never impact scenes or are circumvented without consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual/mechanical elements to enrich magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Add distinctive visual or mechanical rituals (e.g., 'weaving' threads) to make magic memorable and integrated with world lore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual components create evocative imagery and can tie magic to cosmology (Wheel of Time's weaving). They can also enforce skill/knowledge requirements that reinforce limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the principle beyond magic
rubrics_metrics.description: The law 'limitations over powers' applies to characters, worldbuilding, and plot: what characters can't do or must endure is often more interesting than what they can do easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a general storytelling principle: character flaws, harsh living costs, and difficult goals provide deeper drama than merely listing abilities or advantages.
